newsitem.title: CANADA: Teenagers sought refuge from cult group suicide.
newsitem.headline: Teenagers sought refuge from cult group suicide.

text.p: Three teenagers who survived the weekend group suicide of their parents and three other members of the Solar Temple death cult had been given the choice of living or dying, Quebec police said on Monday.

Police found the charred bodies of the three women and two men on Saturday night in a house owned by a member of the Order of the Solar Temple, an international sect that believes death by ritualized suicide leads to rebirth in a star called "Sirius."

Two victims were the owner of the house, Didier Queze, 39, and his wife, Chantale Goupillot, also 39. Their bodies were found in a second-floor bedroom, laid out on a bed with another couple in the form of a cross.

As firefighters fought the blaze on Saturday, the three teenage children of Queze and Goupillot emerged dazed and shaky from a nearby shed. They appeared heavily drugged and anxiously asked firefighters about the fate of their parents.

The children, a 14-year-old girl and two boys, 13 and 16, told police that their parents had asked them whether they wanted to join the group suicide, which cult members believed was a "departure" to another world, police said.

"On Saturday, the children spoke with their parents and were given the choice of staying or leaving and they chose to take refuge outside the house," Mathias Tellier, a spokesman for the Surete du Quebec, the provincial police force, told Reuters.
"The children took sleeping pills, to lessen their pain or sadness over of what was happening inside the house," Tellier said.
After being examined at the Laval University Hospital Center in Quebec City, the teenagers were turned over to the Quebec Youth protection agency (Direction de Protection de la jeunesse).
"Physically speaking, the kids are doing fine but psychologically speaking, they are traumatized and under a state of shock," agency official Jean Lortie said.
"For us they are orphans and they have no families. Nobody from Switzerland and France has contacted us yet," he said.

The children's parents and three other people -- Suzanne Druau, Goupillot's 63-year-old mother, Bruno Klaus, 49, and Pauline Rioux, 54 -- died after a deliberately set fire burned the inside of the house, police said.

Investigators found propane gas tanks and electric hot plates grouped on the ground floor of the house. A fire accelerant, which may have been gasoline, had been spread around the home. Goupillot was found on a sofa on the ground floor with a plastic bag wrapped over her head.
A Quebec coroner said he expected to have autopsy results of the five victims on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Quebec police said they contacted between 30 and 40 people in Quebec who are believed to still be members of the Solar Temple. French and Swiss authorities have already taken similar measures.

The deaths brought to 74 the known number of fatalities involving members of the Order of the Solar Temple. In October 1994, five people were found in a burned out chalet in Morin Heights, a trendy ski resort in the Laurentians region north of Montreal.
The dead included a couple and their baby, who had been stabbed in the heart.

At almost the same time, 48 bodies were found in a farmhouse and two chalets in the Swiss villages of Cheiry and Granges-sur-Salvan. Some of those victims had been stabbed, poisoned, shot or asphyxiated.
In December 1995, police found 16 charred bodies in a remote area of the French Alps. The victims include three children and Edith Vuarnet, wife of a 1960 Olympic ski champion, and her son Patrick.
